ety.text: From Middle English fever, fevere, from Old English fefer, fefor (“fever”) and Old French fievre (“fever”), from Latin febris (“a fever”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”). Displaced native Old English hriþ (“fever”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Fiewer, German Fieber, Danish feber, Swedish feber.

senses.d: A higher than normal body temperature of a person (or, generally, a mammal), usually caused by disease.
ex: There has been a rise in my fever. I think I've the flu.

senses.d: A state of excitement or anxiety.

ex: She threw up her hands in excitement and the ball of water flew right into the pathway of the fever of stingrays.

senses.d: Sexual attraction towards a specific group of people.
To put into a fever; to affect with fever.
ex: the white hand of a lady fever thee
